You met nhaltjan, the verb that means to do WHAT, back in the questions lesson. It has a twin on the answer side: bitjan, to do THUS, to do like this.

Together they're a question-and-answer pair built straight into the verb system:
Nhaltjan? → do how?
Bitjan. → like this.

And bitjan conjugates like any verb: bitjan (I), biyaku (II, the command form), bitjarra (III), bitjana (IV). So you can order someone to do-like-this:
Nhini galki ŋarrakala biyaku bili! → Stay near me all the time! (there's biyaku, the imperative of bitjan, teamed up with our friend bili)

Think about what a pro-verb is for. In English we have a pale version: do so, do the same. But in an oral culture where teaching happens by SHOWING, dance steps, spear grips, weaving moves, a verb that means exactly do it the way I'm doing it is core vocabulary. Bitjan is demonstration compressed into grammar. It also covers say thus, because quoting someone is just doing-like-them with your mouth.

balanya, the adjective twin:
What bitjan is to verbs, balanya is to qualities: like this, of this kind.
Ŋarraku ḻiyapuy balanya → My hat is like this
Ŋayi balanya bili → He is the same (like-this exactly)

nhakuna, the comparator:
And to compare one thing to another, add nhakuna (like, as):
Ŋarraku yiki balanya nhakuna nhuŋu → My knife is like yours
Nhanŋu djorra' ḏarrtjalk balanya nhakuna dhuwala → His book is clean like this one

See the architecture? balanya sets up the of-this-kind-ness, nhakuna points at the standard of comparison. Like...as. The two-part structure will feel familiar from Arabic's مثل or Hebrew's כמו constructions, comparison as pointing, not as adjective-morphing. No -er, no more X than Y machinery. You just say: this-kind, like, that.

Demonstration verbs, demonstration adjectives, comparison by pointing. A grammar built by people who teach with their hands and their country, not with blackboards. When you learn bitjan, you're not learning a word. You're learning how knowledge moves here: watch, then do likewise.
